# The Red and Purple Modernization Program: A Strategic Analysis of Infrastructure Renewal, Urban Resiliency, and Transit-Oriented Evolution in Chicago
## 1\. Introduction: The Imperative for Modernization
### 1.1 The Historical Backbone of the North Side
The Chicago Transit Authority’s (CTA) Red Line is not merely a transportation asset; it is the central nervous system of Chicago’s North Side. Historically providing nearly 67 million rides annually, the Red Line serves some of the most densely populated and economically vital neighborhoods in the United States . For over a century, the North Side Main Line—the four-track corridor stretching north from Belmont Avenue to the city limits—has facilitated the movement of millions, linking the residential districts of Edgewater, Uptown, and Lakeview with the commercial core of the Loop.

However, the physical infrastructure supporting this critical artery dates back to the pre-automotive era. Constructed largely between 1900 and 1924, the steel viaducts, earthen embankments, and retaining walls that characterize the corridor were built during the administrations of presidents like William McKinley and Calvin Coolidge . By the early 21st century, this infrastructure had not only exceeded its intended design life but had become a liability. The structural degradation of the embankment walls and the fatigue of the steel bridges necessitated frequent, costly maintenance and the imposition of "slow zones"—speed restrictions that degraded service reliability and increased travel times for commuters .

The operational limitations were compounded by geometric obsolescence. The system was designed for the ridership patterns of the early 20th century, not the crushing demand of the modern era. In the five-year period leading up to the project's inception, morning and evening rush period ridership on the corridor increased by nearly 40 percent . The existing infrastructure, particularly the complex junctions and century-old signal systems, lacked the capacity to absorb this growth. The CTA faced a critical juncture: without massive intervention, the system would reach a hard capacity ceiling, unable to add the trains necessary to relieve overcrowding, leading to a progressive decline in service quality and passenger comfort .

### 1.2 The "Red Ahead" Vision and Strategic Goals
In response to these challenges, the CTA formulated "Red Ahead," a comprehensive, multi-decade initiative designed to maintain, modernize, and expand the Red Line . The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) program is the crown jewel of this initiative. It is not simply a maintenance project; it is a total reconstruction of the transit environment. The strategic goals of the RPM program are multifaceted:

1. **Capacity Expansion:** The primary operational directive is to unblock the bottlenecks that limit train frequency. By untangling track configurations and upgrading signals, the project aims to significantly increase throughput . 
2. **Speed and Reliability:** The elimination of slow zones and the straightening of track curves are intended to increase commercial speeds and reduce the variance in travel times . 
3. **Universal Accessibility:** A core social mandate of the project is to achieve 100% compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The legacy stations in the corridor, accessible only by stairs, effectively excluded persons with mobility impairments. The RPM program commits to installing elevators and escalators at all reconstructed stations . 
4. **Community and Economic Development:** Beyond the rails, the project seeks to stimulate local economies through Transit-Oriented Development (TOD), creating new public spaces, and supporting local businesses during and after construction .

The RPM program is executed in phases. Phase One, the subject of this detailed analysis, targets the most acute deficiencies in the corridor: the bottleneck at Clark Junction and the deteriorating stations and structures between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr .

## 2\. Phase One Engineering: The Red-Purple Bypass
### 2.1 The Operational Bottleneck at Clark Junction
To understand the engineering necessity of the Red-Purple Bypass, one must first appreciate the operational constraints of the legacy infrastructure. Located just north of the Belmont station, Clark Junction was historically a flat (level) junction where the tracks of the Red, Purple, and Brown Lines intersected .

In this configuration, northbound Brown Line trains—destined for the Ravenswood branch—had to physically cross over the northbound and southbound tracks of the Red and Purple Lines to diverge west. This maneuver was the rail equivalent of a left turn across three lanes of oncoming highway traffic. Whenever a Brown Line train crossed the junction, all Red and Purple Line traffic had to come to a halt. This created a profound choke point.

The CTA’s analysis indicated that this conflict was the single largest constraint on capacity for the entire North Side rail network. During peak periods, the sheer volume of trains meant that delays were endemic. Furthermore, the constraint was absolute; signaling improvements alone could not overcome the physics of two trains needing to occupy the same space at the same time. Modeling suggested that advanced signaling without the physical bypass would allow for the addition of only one extra train per hour. In contrast, the physical separation of the tracks provided by a bypass would allow for up to eight additional trains per hour .

### 2.2 The "Flying Junction" Solution
The solution implemented in Phase One was the construction of a "flying junction," known as the Red-Purple Bypass. This engineering feat involved building a new, elevated track structure that lifts the northbound Brown Line trains *over* the Red and Purple Line tracks.

By vertically separating the conflicting movements, the bypass eliminated the need for Red and Purple trains to stop for diverging Brown Line trains. This grade separation is standard in modern high-capacity metro systems but was a significant undertaking to retrofit into the dense built environment of Chicago’s Lakeview neighborhood.

### 2.3 Construction Methodology and Execution
Construction of the bypass began in the fall of 2019 . The process was surgically precise, necessitated by the need to maintain rail service on the existing tracks while the new structure rose around them. The CTA and its contractor, the Walsh-Fluor Design-Build Team, utilized deep foundation techniques to install the support columns for the new flyover with minimal vibration and disruption to the adjacent buildings .

The bypass structure itself utilizes modern steel and concrete composite designs to dampen noise and vibration—a critical consideration given that the tracks run through a residential alleyway. The new northbound Brown Line track on the bypass was completed and opened to revenue service in November 2021 . This milestone was pivotal. Once the Brown Line trains were moved to the high-level bypass, the old flat junction tracks could be decommissioned, clearing the way for the subsequent reconstruction of the Red and Purple Line tracks below.

### 2.4 The Historic Vautravers Building Relocation
The construction of the bypass required straightening the alignment of the tracks north of Belmont to allow for higher speeds. Directly in the path of this new alignment stood the Vautravers Building, a historic three-story greystone located at 947-949 W. Newport Avenue . Built between 1891 and 1894, the building is a contributing structure to the Newport Avenue Historic District and a cherished piece of the neighborhood’s architectural fabric .

Faced with the choice between demolition (which would compromise the historic district) and a costly relocation, the CTA chose the latter, demonstrating a nuanced approach to heritage conservation.

* **Preparation:** In the months leading up to the move, crews engaged in extensive preparatory work. This included removing the limestone cladding and Chicago common brick from the façade to prevent damage, excavating around the foundation, and installing a complex system of temporary bracing . 
* **The Move:** In August 2021, the entire 127-year-old building was lifted onto a system of hydraulic push rams and roll beams. Over the course of the operation, the building was slid approximately 30 feet to the west and placed on a new foundation . 
* **Investment:** The CTA purchased the property for $1.75 million and invested an additional $1.75 million to execute the move and restore the structure, ensuring it would continue to serve as a residential building safely outside the new track alignment .

## 3\. Phase One Engineering: Lawrence to Bryn Mawr Modernization
### 3.1 Corridor Reconstruction and Embankment Removal
The second, and physically larger, component of RPM Phase One is the Lawrence to Bryn Mawr Modernization (LBMM). This segment involves the complete demolition and reconstruction of 1.3 miles of the four-track main line through the Uptown and Edgewater neighborhoods .

The legacy infrastructure here consisted of tracks running on an earthen embankment contained by concrete retaining walls, interrupted by steel viaduct bridges at street crossings. These structures, built in the early 1920s, were rapidly deteriorating. The retaining walls showed signs of distress, and the viaducts required constant shoring.

The modernization project replaces this entire assembly with a modern, closed-deck aerial track structure . Unlike the open-deck steel bridges of the past, which allowed train noise to cascade down to the street, the new structure features a concrete deck with integrated noise barriers. This design significantly reduces the acoustic signature of the trains, improving the quality of life for residents living adjacent to the "L" . Furthermore, the removal of the solid earthen embankment eliminates the "wall" that divided the neighborhood for a century, opening up the ground level for light, air, and public use .

### 3.2 Two-Stage Construction Strategy
Rebuilding a busy four-track railroad without suspending service required a complex staging plan. The project adopted a longitudinal split strategy:

* **Stage A (2021-2023):** Construction crews first demolished the two easternmost tracks (typically the northbound Red and Purple lines). During this period, all train traffic—northbound and southbound—was consolidated onto the two remaining western tracks. This allowed the contractor to build the new eastern half of the viaduct and the new northbound platforms . Stage A was completed in July 2023, marked by the activation of the new northbound tracks . 
* **Stage B (2023-2025):** Following the completion of Stage A, traffic was shifted onto the newly built eastern tracks. Crews then proceeded to demolish the old western tracks and embankment. As of late 2024, construction is proceeding on the western half of the structure and the southbound station houses. This stage is scheduled for substantial completion in 2025 .

### 3.3 Station Architecture and Accessibility
The project includes the demolition and replacement of four stations: Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr. The old stations were cramped, dark, and inaccessible to people with disabilities. The new stations are designed as modern civic gateways.

* **Lawrence and Berwyn:** These stations are being rebuilt with wider platforms, better lighting, and full ADA accessibility. 
* **Argyle and Bryn Mawr:** These stops will also feature new accessible entrances. The new Bryn Mawr station, for instance, will include a new entrance at Hollywood Avenue to better serve the northern end of the platform . 
* **Design Features:** The new stations incorporate 100% vertical accessibility via elevators and escalators . They feature "Train Tracker" digital screens for real-time arrival information, vastly improved security lighting, and integrated public art installations . The platforms are wider to accommodate modern ridership levels and prevent the dangerous crowding that occurred at the old stations .

### 3.4 Temporary Stations and Service Continuity
To maintain access during the multi-year construction process, the CTA constructed temporary stations. During Stage A, temporary stations were used at Argyle and Bryn Mawr. When Stage B began in July 2023, the temporary station configurations were adjusted. For example, the new temporary Argyle station utilized entrances on West Foster and West Winona, while the temporary Bryn Mawr station shifted to minimize walking distances for customers . This commitment to keeping the stations open—rather than utilizing bus replacements for years—was a critical requirement for the community, ensuring that residents could still access the rail network despite the heavy construction .

## 4\. Systems Modernization: Signals and Power
### 4.1 The Nervous System of the "L"
While concrete and steel are the visible elements of modernization, the RPM program also includes a comprehensive overhaul of the corridor's "nervous system"—the signals and traction power network.

The project scope includes the installation of a new signal system along 23 track miles from Howard to Belmont . The legacy system was a fixed-block system with technology dating back decades. The new system is designed to improve train flow and service reliability. While the snippets do not explicitly confirm a transition to Moving Block Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC), they describe the system as improving flow "similar to roadway traffic signals" and utilizing "audio frequency" technology .

### 4.2 Signal Technology Nuances
Industry discussions surrounding the project indicate a move toward advanced audio frequency track circuits. This technology offers a significant upgrade over older DC track circuits by providing more granular train detection and higher immunity to electrical interference. The new system allows for tighter headways (the time interval between trains) and more consistent speeds, reducing the "stop-and-go" operation that frustrates passengers . This signal upgrade acts as a force multiplier for the physical infrastructure; the flyover provides the space for more trains, and the new signals provide the control logic to run them safely and efficiently.

### 4.3 Power Distribution
Supporting the increased service levels requires a robust power supply. The RPM program and parallel CTA initiatives involve upgrading traction power substations. For example, the overarching capital budget includes funding for new substations at Barry and Damen (on the Blue Line, but indicative of the system-wide power upgrades) and upgrades to the corridor's electrical backbone to handle the load of additional trains .

## 5\. Financial Architecture: A Multi-Source Funding Strategy
### 5.1 The Funding "Lasagne"
The Phase One project cost is approximately $2.1 billion . Financing a project of this magnitude required the CTA to assemble a complex "lasagne" of funding sources, blending federal grants with innovative local value-capture mechanisms.

**Table 1: RPM Phase One Funding Structure**

| Funding Source | Amount (Approx.) | Mechanism and Details |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **FTA Core Capacity Grant** | $957 Million | A federal discretionary grant specifically for projects that increase capacity in existing corridors. Awarded via a Full Funding Grant Agreement (FFGA) in Jan 2017 |
| **Transit TIF** | $622 Million | Revenue generated from the dedicated Red-Purple Modernization Transit Tax Increment Financing district |
| **CMAQ Grant** | $125 Million | Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality Improvement grant, focused on environmental benefits |
| **CTA Financing** | \~$400 Million | Includes CTA sales tax revenue bonds and other local financing tools |

### 5.2 The Innovation of Transit TIF
The Transit Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district represents a significant policy innovation. Traditionally, TIFs in Chicago were used for neighborhood redevelopment, often diverting property tax growth from schools and other taxing bodies to fund local amenities. This led to controversy.

The **Transit TIF**, authorized by the Illinois General Assembly in 2016 specifically for this project, operates differently. It captures the increment of property tax value growth *only* from the properties that benefit directly from the transit improvement (defined as the area roughly 0.5 miles from the line) . The RPM Transit TIF district covers 3,126 acres from Devon Avenue to North Avenue . Crucially, the legislation was crafted to ensure that the impact on Chicago Public Schools was minimized compared to traditional TIFs.

This $622 million local contribution was the key that unlocked the federal matching funds. The FTA requires a substantial local match to award Core Capacity grants; the Transit TIF provided a dedicated, reliable revenue stream that proved the CTA’s ability to pay its share . The funds from the TIF are primarily used to service the debt on the TIFIA loans and bonds issued to pay for upfront construction costs.

### 5.3 Federal Partnership
The $957 million Core Capacity grant was the largest such grant in CTA history at the time. It signaled a federal recognition of the Red Line’s national importance. The grant agreement, signed in the waning days of the Obama administration in January 2017, locked in the federal commitment, protecting the project from potential shifts in transportation policy .

## 6\. Urban Integration: "Under the L" and Placemaking
### 6.1 Creating New Public Space
Perhaps the most visible urban design impact of the RPM project is the creation of new public land. By demolishing the solid earthen embankment that carried the tracks between Lawrence and Ardmore, the CTA has effectively "found" 10 blocks of open space that previously did not exist as accessible land .

This 1.3-mile strip of land, located directly beneath the new aerial track structure, presents a unique opportunity for placemaking. The CTA refers to this initiative as the "Under the 'L' Experience" .

### 6.2 Community-Driven Design Process
Recognizing that this space serves the immediate neighborhoods of Uptown and Edgewater, the CTA engaged in a rigorous public design process.

* **Engagement:** In early 2024, the CTA and its landscape architecture partner, Site Design Group, held multiple rounds of public meetings (January and May) to solicit ideas from residents . 
* **Concepts:** The community feedback led to a diverse menu of proposed amenities. The preliminary designs unveiled in May 2024 include pedestrian trails, dog parks, playgrounds for children, outdoor fitness areas, and flexible plazas capable of hosting farmers' markets or community festivals . 
* **Activation Framework:** The "Public Space Activation Framework" report outlines the governance and maintenance strategies for these spaces, ensuring they remain vibrant community assets rather than neglected under-bridge areas .

### 6.3 Implementation Timeline
The construction of these community spaces is sequenced to follow the heavy civil engineering work. With the track structure expected to be complete in 2025, the "Under the L" construction is scheduled to begin in 2026 and conclude in 2027 . This staggering ensures that the delicate landscape work is not damaged by the heavy machinery required for the rail viaducts.

## 7\. Socio-Economic Impacts and Community Relations
### 7.1 The Gentrification Debate
Major transit investments inevitably alter the economic value of the surrounding land. The RPM project has been a focal point for debates regarding gentrification in the North Side neighborhoods.

* **Community Concerns:** Organizations like ONE Northside have expressed concern that the "shiny new" infrastructure serves as a beacon for real estate speculation . Critics argue that the project incentivizes developers to purchase aging housing stock—such as the single-room occupancy (SRO) hotels that historically housed low-income residents in Uptown—and convert them into luxury apartments. Anecdotal evidence, such as rent increases at the Lawrence House and other nearby properties, is often cited as a ripple effect of the transit modernization . 
* **Displacement Risks:** Teachers at local schools, such as Goudy Public School, have reported fears that the families of their students will be priced out of the neighborhood as the amenity value of the transit corridor rises .

### 7.2 Mitigation Strategies: Equitable Transit-Oriented Development (eTOD)
The CTA and the City of Chicago have attempted to address these concerns through policy planning.

* **Surplus Land:** The project required the acquisition and demolition of certain properties to widen the right-of-way. Once construction is complete, the CTA will own surplus parcels of land. The agency has committed to an Equitable Transit-Oriented Development (eTOD) plan for these sites . 
* **RFP Process:** The CTA intends to issue Requests for Proposals (RFPs) for the redevelopment of these parcels. The eTOD plan serves as a guide, encouraging proposals that include affordable housing, local retail, and community services, rather than maximizing profit through luxury condos alone . 
* **Business Support:** Recognizing that construction disruption can be fatal to small businesses, the CTA launched the "Open for Business" campaign. This initiative engaged local Chambers of Commerce to promote businesses impacted by the work, encouraging riders to "Shop, Eat, Play, Explore" in the construction zones .

## 8\. Future Trajectory: The Next Phases
### 8.1 Beyond Phase One
Phase One addresses only a fraction of the 9.6-mile corridor. The "Red Ahead" vision encompasses the entire line north to the Linden terminal in Wilmette. The CTA is currently advancing the **RPM Next Phases Planning Study**, which covers the remaining territory .

### 8.2 The Three Segments
The Next Phases study divides the remaining work into three geographic segments:

1. **Addison to Sheridan:** This segment connects the southern end of the Phase One project (at the new Bypass) to the northern end of the Phase One project (near Bryn Mawr). It includes the busy Sheridan station and the tracks through the Buena Park neighborhood . 
2. **Thorndale to Howard:** This segment extends from the northern limit of Phase One to the Howard terminal, the transfer point for the Yellow and Purple lines . 
3. **Evanston Branch:** This covers the Purple Line from Howard north to the Linden terminal, involving the replacement of aging viaducts and embankments in Evanston and Wilmette .

### 8.3 Planning Status and Funding Outlook
The planning study, initiated in 2021, is expected to be finalized in 2025 . This study will identify the "Preferred Alternative" for these segments, a necessary step to clear the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process.

* **Status:** As of 2025, the CTA is applying for funding to manage the NEPA process for Phase Two . 
* **The Fiscal Cliff:** The path to construction for these future phases is clouded by the region's broader transit funding crisis. The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) projects a massive operating budget shortfall starting in 2026 . While capital funds (for building) are legally distinct from operating funds (for running trains), the overall fiscal health of the agency is a major variable. The CTA has warned that without a new capital funding source—similar to the state "Rebuild Illinois" bond program or a new federal infrastructure package—the timeline for Phase Two remains uncertain .

## 9\. Conclusion
The Red and Purple Modernization Program Phase One stands as a defining moment in the history of Chicago’s infrastructure. It represents the transition of the "L" from a legacy system, constrained by the engineering limitations of the 1900s, to a modern, high-capacity metro capable of serving the city for another century.

The engineering triumphs of the project—the surgical insertion of the Red-Purple Bypass and the "Under the L" transformation—demonstrate a sophisticated approach to urban problem-solving. The CTA has managed to execute a multi-billion dollar rebuild while maintaining service, preserving heritage structures like the Vautravers building, and creating new public realms.

However, the project also highlights the complex socio-economic dynamics of transit investment. The tension between modernization and gentrification remains a critical challenge, one that the CTA’s eTOD policies will need to address aggressively in the post-construction years.

As Phase One nears its completion in July 2025, the physical landscape of the North Side will be irrevocably changed. The rust-stained retaining walls and deafening steel bridges will be gone, replaced by a quieter, faster, and more accessible system. The challenge for the region now shifts to the future: securing the political and financial capital necessary to extend this modernization to the remaining miles of the Red and Purple lines, ensuring that the benefits of this renewal are felt from Belmont all the way to Linden.

Transit TIF provided $622 Million in revenue generated from the dedicated Red-Purple Modernization Transit Tax Increment Financing district.
CMAQ Grant provided $125 Million, focused on environmental benefits.
CTA Financing provided approximately $400 Million, including CTA sales tax revenue bonds and other local financing tools.
The Transit Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district represents a significant policy innovation.
Traditionally, TIFs in Chicago were used for neighborhood redevelopment, often diverting property tax growth from schools and other taxing bodies to fund local amenities.
The Transit TIF, authorized by the Illinois General Assembly in 2016 specifically for this project, operates differently.
It captures the increment of property tax value growth only from the properties that benefit directly from the transit improvement (defined as the area roughly 0.5 miles from the line).
The RPM Transit TIF district covers 3,126 acres from Devon Avenue to North Avenue.
The legislation for the Transit TIF was crafted to ensure that the impact on Chicago Public Schools was minimized compared to traditional TIFs.
This $622 million local contribution was the key that unlocked the federal matching funds.
The FTA requires a substantial local match to award Core Capacity grants.
The Transit TIF provided a dedicated, reliable revenue stream that proved the CTA’s ability to pay its share.
The funds from the TIF are primarily used to service the debt on the TIFIA loans and bonds issued to pay for upfront construction costs.
The $957 million Core Capacity grant was the largest such grant in CTA history at the time.
It signaled a federal recognition of the Red Line’s national importance.
The grant agreement, signed in the waning days of the Obama administration in January 2017, locked in the federal commitment, protecting the project from potential shifts in transportation policy.
The most visible urban design impact of the RPM project is the creation of new public land.

By demolishing the solid earthen embankment that carried the tracks between Lawrence and Ardmore, the CTA has effectively "found" 10 blocks of open space that previously did not exist as accessible land.
This 1.3-mile strip of land, located directly beneath the new aerial track structure, presents a unique opportunity for placemaking.
The CTA refers to this initiative as the "Under the 'L' Experience".
Recognizing that this space serves the immediate neighborhoods of Uptown and Edgewater, the CTA engaged in a rigorous public design process.
In early 2024, the CTA and its landscape architecture partner, Site Design Group, held multiple rounds of public meetings (January and May) to solicit ideas from residents.
The community feedback led to a diverse menu of proposed amenities.

The preliminary designs unveiled in May 2024 include pedestrian trails, dog parks, playgrounds for children, outdoor fitness areas, and flexible plazas capable of hosting farmers' markets or community festivals.

The "Public Space Activation Framework" report outlines the governance and maintenance strategies for these spaces, ensuring they remain vibrant community assets rather than neglected under-bridge areas.
The construction of these community spaces is sequenced to follow the heavy civil engineering work.
With the track structure expected to be complete in 2025, the "Under the L" construction is scheduled to begin in 2026 and conclude in 2027.
This staggering ensures that the delicate landscape work is not damaged by the heavy machinery required for the rail viaducts.
Major transit investments inevitably alter the economic value of the surrounding land.
The RPM project has been a focal point for debates regarding gentrification in the North Side neighborhoods.
Organizations like ONE Northside have expressed concern that the "shiny new" infrastructure serves as a beacon for real estate speculation.

Critics argue that the project incentivizes developers to purchase aging housing stock—such as the single-room occupancy (SRO) hotels that historically housed low-income residents in Uptown—and convert them into luxury apartments.
Anecdotal evidence, such as rent increases at the Lawrence House and other nearby properties, is often cited as a ripple effect of the transit modernization.

Teachers at local schools, such as Goudy Public School, have reported fears that the families of their students will be priced out of the neighborhood as the amenity value of the transit corridor rises.
The CTA and the City of Chicago have attempted to address these concerns through policy planning.
The project required the acquisition and demolition of certain properties to widen the right-of-way.
Once construction is complete, the CTA will own surplus parcels of land.
The agency has committed to an Equitable Transit-Oriented Development (eTOD) plan for these sites.
The CTA intends to issue Requests for Proposals (RFPs) for the redevelopment of these parcels.
The eTOD plan serves as a guide, encouraging proposals that include affordable housing, local retail, and community services, rather than maximizing profit through luxury condos alone.
Recognizing that construction disruption can be fatal to small businesses, the CTA launched the "Open for Business" campaign.
This initiative engaged local Chambers of Commerce to promote businesses impacted by the work, encouraging riders to "Shop, Eat, Play, Explore" in the construction zones.
Phase One addresses only a fraction of the 9.6-mile corridor.
The "Red Ahead" vision encompasses the entire line north to the Linden terminal in Wilmette.
The CTA is currently advancing the RPM Next Phases Planning Study, which covers the remaining territory.
The Next Phases study divides the remaining work into three geographic segments.
The first segment, Addison to Sheridan, connects the southern end of the Phase One project (at the new Bypass) to the northern end of the Phase One project (near Bryn Mawr).
This segment includes the busy Sheridan station and the tracks through the Buena Park neighborhood.
The second segment, Thorndale to Howard, extends from the northern limit of Phase One to the Howard terminal, the transfer point for the Yellow and Purple lines.
The third segment, Evanston Branch, covers the Purple Line from Howard north to the Linden terminal, involving the replacement of aging viaducts and embankments in Evanston and Wilmette.
The planning study, initiated in 2021, is expected to be finalized in 2025.
This study will identify the "Preferred Alternative" for these segments, a necessary step to clear the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process.
As of 2025, the CTA is applying for funding to manage the NEPA process for Phase Two.
The path to construction for these future phases is clouded by the region's broader transit funding crisis.
The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) projects a massive operating budget shortfall starting in 2026.
While capital funds (for building) are legally distinct from operating funds (for running trains), the overall fiscal health of the agency is a major variable.
The CTA has warned that without a new capital funding source—similar to the state "Rebuild Illinois" bond program or a new federal infrastructure package—the timeline for Phase Two remains uncertain.
The Red and Purple Modernization Program Phase One stands as a defining moment in the history of Chicago’s infrastructure.

It represents the transition of the "L" from a legacy system, constrained by the engineering limitations of the 1900s, to a modern, high-capacity metro capable of serving the city for another century.
The engineering triumphs of the project—the surgical insertion of the Red-Purple Bypass and the "Under the L" transformation—demonstrate a sophisticated approach to urban problem-solving.
The CTA has managed to execute a multi-billion dollar rebuild while maintaining service, preserving heritage structures like the Vautravers building, and creating new public realms.
The project also highlights the complex socio-economic dynamics of transit investment.
The tension between modernization and gentrification remains a critical challenge, one that the CTA’s eTOD policies will need to address aggressively in the post-construction years.
As Phase One nears its completion in July 2025, the physical landscape of the North Side will be irrevocably changed.
The rust-stained retaining walls and deafening steel bridges will be gone, replaced by a quieter, faster, and more accessible system.

The challenge for the region now shifts to the future: securing the political and financial capital necessary to extend this modernization to the remaining miles of the Red and Purple lines, ensuring that the benefits of this renewal are felt from Belmont all the way to Linden.

2.content:
Rebuilding vital infrastructure for Chicago’s future
----------------------------------------------------

The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) corridor is a 9.6-mile stretch of track that was built close to a century ago—much of it in 1924, when Calvin Coolidge was U.S. President and the Wrigley Building had just been constructed. Most of this infrastructure is at the end of its useful lifespan. Frequent maintenance to repair tracks and remove slow zones is costly and hinders service.

RPM Phase One:

*   [Lawrence to Bryn Mawr 3D animation (2020)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RVsP9DjTYW4)
*   [Red-Purple Bypass 3D animation (2020)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FMJ1TWFDwJ0&feature=youtu.be)

### Significant ridership, population growth

The Red Line is now Chicago’s busiest ‘L’ line, serving some of the most densely populated neighborhoods in the country, and the number of riders along this corridor is only growing. Morning and evening rush period ridership increased by nearly 40 percent over a five-year period.

CTA needs to increase service on the Red Line to serve more riders. However, with current infrastructure constraints, the Red Line has reached capacity, which means we cannot add more trains during rush periods. If nothing is done, CTA will continue to be unable to add more trains to accommodate riders, trains will become more overcrowded, and passengers wait times will increase.

![Image 1: 2015rpm ridership bar chart](https://bondlink-cdn.com/6156/2015rpm_ridership_bar_chart-cropped.KnJvM1CRd.jpg)

### RPM: Meeting future ridership demand

In order to completely rebuild and modernize the stations, tracks and infrastructure along this corridor, we must be able to improve the efficiency of our operations to be able to increase the number of trains to meeting ridership demand today and in the future.

Rebuilding and modernizing the Red Line stations alone will not be enough to meet our future capacity needs. The proposed Red-Purple Bypass is also necessary to increase train service over the next 60 to 80 years.

### RPM Phase One

The comprehensive work that will be performed under the RPM program is scheduled to be completed in phases, which allows us to make the greatest number of improvements while minimizing impacts on riders and the surrounding communities.

**Phase One includes two main components:**

*   [Red-Purple Bypass Project](https://www.transitchicago.com/rpmproject/bypass/)
*   [Lawrence to Bryn Mawr Modernization Project](https://www.transitchicago.com/rpmproject/lawrmawr/)

### Scope

RPM Phase One will completely rebuild the Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn and Bryn Mawr stations and all the tracks and support structures for more than a mile adjacent to the stations. The stations will be accessible for the first time and include wider platforms, better lighting and modern amenities. The project will also construct a Red-Purple Bypass north of Belmont station trains to modernize the century-old Clark Junction where Red, Purple and Brown Line trains currently intersect. The bypass, which will carry northbound Brown Line trains up and over Red and Purple Line tracks,will eliminate the need for trains to stop and wait for other trains to cross, thereby allowing CTA to significantly increase the number of trains it runs along the Red Line --reducing overcrowding and meeting growing demand for transit service.

### How will we pay for it?

RPM Phase One is funded by $957 million from federal Core Capacity Funds that was formally approved by a Full Funding Grant Agreement with the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) on Jan. 9, 2017. The remaining Phase One funding includes a federal $125 million Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality Improvement (CMAQ) grant from the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning (CMAP), $622 million in Transit TIF funds from the City of Chicago and CTA financing.

### Program History

The RPM Program has evolved through a series of studies and public outreach processes that have shaped the development of the program over time.

![Image 2: timeline graphic (2)](https://bondlink-cdn.com/6156/timeline_graphic_-2--cropped.xs8RdNL4R.jpg)

**2009-2010:** CTA conducted a vision study between fall 2009 and fall 2010 to understand the public’s priorities and concerns, conduct an existing conditions analysis, and frame project alternatives. The analysis helped define the purpose and need and included a high-level evaluation of potential improvements to the corridor. The process included four public meetings attended by over 300 people, a website, a comment period, and a direct mail survey sent to over 11,000 residents and businesses along the corridor.

**2011:** In January 2011, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) scoping process began. The purpose of this process was to inform the public about the project and gather input on the scope of the environmental studies, draft purpose and need statement, and alternatives to be evaluated. Four public scoping meetings provided the public with an opportunity to comment on the project purpose and need, alternatives to be considered, and issues and areas of concern to be considered in the Draft Environmental Impact Statement for the entire 9.6-mile RPM corridor.

**2012:** CTA held two community update meetings in early 2012, which allowed attendees to learn about refined alternatives for the RPM corridor based on public scoping, review project information, and clarify their understanding of the project and environmental process.

**2013:** During 2013, CTA conducted additional research and a conceptual design process to look at ways to further minimize environmental impacts. In late 2013, FTA and CTA developed a tailored approach for phased improvements to the RPM corridor.

**2014:** CTA announced the RPM Phase One projects to the public in April 2014. Throughout spring and summer 2014, CTA held a number of focused community group meetings and public open houses. These meetings were conducted to gather feedback from the public on the proposed improvements and determine areas of concern to be analyzed and documented within the RPM Phase One Environmental Assessments (EAs).

**2015:** CTA held public hearings for the Lawrence to Bryn Mawr Modernization Project and Red-Purple Bypass Project EAs in May and June 2015, and established a 30-day public comment period to accept comments for each project. Based on a review of all comments received, FTA will issue a final NEPA environmental decision document for each RPM Phase One project. This finding will guide future implementation of these projects. FTA issued a Finding of No Significant Impact for the Lawrence to Bryn Mawr Modernization Project on October 2, 2015.

**2016:** In 2016, CTA formally applied for federal funding and also secured local funding through the Transit TIF.

**2017:** On Jan. 9, 2017, CTA signed the Full Funding Grant Agreement with the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) that is the final step in securing the funding needed for the $2.1 billion first phase of the RPM project.

**2018:** CTA began property demolition and advance utility relocation work in preparation for construction of the RPM Phase One project. In December 2018, CTA awarded a contract to design and build the project to Walsh-Fluor Design-Build Team, following an 18-month Request for Qualifications (RFQ) and Request for Proposals (RFP) process.

**2019:** CTA in February 2019 issued a Notice to Proceed to Walsh-Fluor to begin work on the project. CTA broke ground on the Red-Purple Bypass in October 2019 and in December 2019 began "pre-stage" preparatory trackwork for the Lawrence to Bryn Mawr corridor, ahead of new station and track construction starting in 2021.

**2020:** CTA continues to build the Red-Purple Bypass rail bridge. Simultaneously, the CTA continues performing extensive "pre-stage" work to the Red and Purple Line tracks to allow the CTA to provide Red and Purple Line service on two tracks instead of the usual four tracks, because CTA will be rebuilding two tracks at a time along with new stations between 2021-2024.

CTA’s Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project’s Final Major Stage of North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction to Begin This Fall
============================================================================================================================================

 September 26, 2023 

 September 26, 2023 

 Staff 

_**RPM project to reach next major milestone following completion of new track structure north of Belmont station marking the project being two-thirds complete; community meeting to be held 10/17**_

The Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) today announced the agency will begin this fall the final major stage of the North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction project as part of CTA’s Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project. This final stage will mark the next major milestone for the RPM project, completing new elevated track structure north of Belmont station and reaching the two-thirds completion point for this section of the project.

The North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction project includes two major components: the new Red-Purple Bypass, which opened in November 2021, and the full reconstruction of the 0.3 miles of southbound track structure north of Belmont station to approximately Newport/Cornelia avenues south of Addison Red Line station. The bypass, along with the new Red and Purple line tracks being finished this fall, allow trains to travel more efficiently with fewer delays, and provide CTA with additional capacity to add trains to meet ridership demand.

“As CTA ridership returns in record numbers nearing pre-pandemic levels, we are pleased to deliver modern track infrastructure to our customers,” said CTA President Dorval R. Carter, Jr. “Combined with the new tracks recently opened between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr earlier this year, we have now built nearly two miles of new tracks under the RPM project. We look forward to continuing to deliver on our promises to modernize the Red Line from north to south.”

### Final major stage of North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction (fall 2023 through 2025)

With the completion of the bypass and the new southbound Red and Purple line tracks, CTA can move on to the next phase of work. CTA’s RPM project contractor, Walsh-Fluor, will rebuild 0.3 miles of northbound Red and Purple Line elevated track structures between Belmont station on the south to the stretch of track between Newport and Cornelia avenues on the north.

*   Reconstruction of southbound tracks began in late 2021 and will be completed late 2023.
*   Reconstruction of northbound tracks will start late 2023 and is expected to be completed in 2025.

### Minor rail service impacts expected in fall 2023

Red, Purple and Brown Line service will be maintained through the end of the project in 2025, with minor interruptions at the time of the new tracks being put into service this fall. During the weekends when rail service is interrupted, CTA will provide free shuttle buses between stations for customers. Upcoming scheduled service* interruptions:

*   Brown Line: Belmont to Southport interrupted Oct. 14-16
*   Red and Purple Line: Belmont to Addison interrupted Oct. 27-30 and Nov. 10-13

_*Construction schedules are subject to change._

### Community meeting: North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction

CTA and Walsh-Fluor hold an in-person public meeting and will also be recorded and posted on our web site. Register for the meeting [here.](https://www.eventbrite.com/e/its-time-the-final-stage-of-the-north-belmont-red-purple-reconstruction-tickets-726324876257)

**October 17**

Second Unitarian Church of Chicago, 656 W Barry Ave

5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.

Translation services will be available upon request.

### RPM Phase One Overview

RPM Phase One Project includes three major components:

*   Reconstruction of the Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr Red Line stations into larger, 100 percent accessible stations; and replacement of track structure totaling six track-miles (ongoing).
*   New Red-Purple Bypass construction (completed in 2021) and the reconstruction of Red and Purple Line track structure between Belmont and Newport/Cornelia (ongoing).
*   Installation of a new signal system on 23 track miles between Howard and Belmont that, similar to roadway traffic signals, will improve train flow and service reliability (ongoing).

### The Red Line and RPM

The CTA’s Red Line is CTA’s busiest rail line, historically providing more than 67 million rides a year and serving some of the most densely populated neighborhoods in U.S.

The RPM Program, which will be done in multiple phases, will rebuild the 9.6-mile stretch of Red and Purple Line track structure and stations on the North Side that are a century old. RPM will replace aging infrastructure; increase CTA’s capacity to increase train service as needed; and improve our service for customers with more reliable, comfortable service. Future phases of RPM have not yet been announced and are currently unfunded. For more information on RPM Next Phases, please visit [transitchicago.com/rpm/next-phases](https://www.transitchicago.com/rpm/next-phases/).

Learn more about RPM online at transitchicago.com/RPM and sign up for project alerts at transitchicago.com/RPMalerts.

# Red-Purple Bypass Project Purpose and Need 

Project Purpose 

The purpose of the Red-Purple Bypass Project is to improve capacity, travel time, ride quality, and safety in one of CTA’s highest ridership corridors. The project would allow CTA to increase functional capacity to meet ridership demands while maintaining or improving the quality, speed, and passenger comfort. 

Needs to be Addressed 

• A substantial number of transit customers rely on the existing train line • Peak ridership demand exceeds existing infrastructure capacity • Passenger crowding is common on trains and delays occur frequently • Train speeds are reduced due to cross traffic and antiquated infrastructure • Existing infrastructure is substantially past its useful life • Maintaining safe operating conditions becomes more difficult and costly as the infrastructure ages and deteriorates The Environmental Assessment describes the purpose and need for this project and evidence supporting the needs identified. Alternatives Development Process • Vision study for 9.6-mile RPM corridor • 4 public meetings, over 300 public comments, over 11,000 mailed surveys 2009 – 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 – Present • NEPA* scoping process for 9.6-mile RPM corridor • 4 public meetings, over 1,500 public comments • Refined alternatives • Bypass at Clark Junction introduced • 2 public meetings • Research, concept design to reduce impacts • FTA and CTA defined a phased approach for the RPM Program • Announced Build Alternative to public • Public meetings held to gather input on proposed improvements and areas of concern 

> *National Environmental Policy Act

# Alternatives Studied and Eliminated Underground Tunnel (Subway) 

Major Reasons for Elimination • Substantially larger project footprint • Greater impacts on properties and the community • Longer construction duration and greater costs • Substantial service disruption during construction • Would not allow phasing of the RPM Program 

Track 4 Bypass 

Major Reasons for Elimination • Would not eliminate property impacts • Introduces a new capacity constraint in the system • Would not meet purpose and need for the project 

Bypass using Center Tracks 

Major Reasons for Elimination • Would not eliminate property impacts • Severe operational impacts during construction • Bus shuttles would be insufficient to meet passenger needs during construction • Would not meet the purpose and need for the project 

Stacking Tracks 

Major Reasons for Elimination • Longer project length required • Wider right-of-way required • Would result in greater property impacts • Substantial operational issues • Visual impact of double-stacked structure Purpose and Status of the Environmental Assessment (EA) EA Purpose 

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) looks at a broad range of community and environmental impacts. It is required for all federally funded projects. 

Section 4(f) Section 6(f) RCRA/CERCLA Endangered Species Act Farmland Protection Policy Act Clean Air Act Clean Water Act Floodplains & Wetlands Environmental Justice Orders National Historic Preservation Act NEPA National Environmental Policy Act 

EA Status 

Red-Purple Bypass Project was published and made available for public review and comment on May 19, 2015. • Comments and responses received on environmental impacts will be incorporated into the final decision document • FTA will issue a finding on the proposed project based on the significance of impacts identified • The finding will guide future planning and implementation of the project Alternatives Considered 

This Environmental Assessment compares the No Build Alternative and Build Alternative for the Red-Purple Bypass Project. 

No Build Alternative 

• Required as part of NEPA environmental analysis • Includes typical ongoing repairs only and represents future condition if the project were not implemented • Compares the relative benefits and impacts of the Build Alternative 

Key Characteristics of the No Build Alternative 

• Does not expand capacity, or improve service quality or travel times • Includes funding for emergency repairs at historic levels • Limited benefits that only provide a short-term extension of structure life 

Build Alternative 

• Construction of a fifth track bypass for the northbound Brown Line • Reconstruction of approximately 0.3 mile of the mainline Red and Purple line tracks from Belmont station on the south to the segment of track between Newport and Cornelia Avenues on the north 

Key Characteristics of the Build Alternative 

• Replacement of the existing flat junction with a new fifth track bypass • Reconstruction of mainline Red and Purple line tracks, removing existing slow curves, and meeting modern design and safety standards • Installation of a closed-deck, aerial track structure with noise barriers to minimize noise impacts • Would address functional and structural capacity issues in the project area for the next 60 to 80 years Fifth Track Bypass Fifth Track Bypass: Build a grade-separated junction allowing northbound Brown Line trains to cross unimpeded over the other tracks on a new aerial structure, resulting in increased capacity for all three lines while also improving travel time and overall system reliability and safety. 

Key Benefits 

• Removes the largest physical constraint (flat junction) in the RPM corridor • Allows CTA to increase peak service on the Red Line by up to 30% • Allows CTA to add up to 8 more trains per hour during rush hour on the Red Line alone • Additional capacity would allow CTA to accommodate up to 7,200 more passengers per hour 

Key Impacts 

• Additional right-of-way required to accommodate new bypass 

How the Build Alternative Reduces Impacts 

• CTA conducted detailed surveys which identified properties that provide enough space for construction, as well as right-of-way  

> Current view of junction north of Belmont Conceptual rendering of the junction north of Belmont

# Mainline Tracks Key Benefits 

• Removes existing speed-restrictive curves to improve speed and ride quality • Meets all modern design standards and improves safety • Minimizes noise and vibration impacts by using a closed-deck structure with welded rail and noise barriers • Together with the new bypass, straightening the curves would save passengers more than ½ million hours in travel time annually 

Key Impacts 

• Additional right-of-way would be required to meet modern track spacing requirements and straighten slow curves 

How the Build Alternative Reduces Impacts 

• Construction would cause limited disruptions to transit service • A closed-deck structure with noise barriers on both sides of the track deck would reduce noise transmission at and below track level

# Permanent Property Displacements Permanent Property Displacements 

Displaced owners will be compensated and provided relocation assistance per the federal Uniform Act. 

Compensation for Property Owners 

• Payment will be no less than fair market value for the owners’ land and buildings • Owners may be eligible for compensation equal to the original purchase price of the property 

Owner and Tenant Relocation 

• Compensation will be provided for the cost of moving your business or residence Community and Business Impacts 

While the permanent result of these improvements is expected to be largely beneficial to the surrounding community, construction could have impacts to the community and particularly surrounding local businesses. CTA proposes to develop a Construction Outreach and Coordination Plan in collaboration with aldermanic offices and surrounding community stakeholders to promote and assist local businesses and residences affected by construction. 

Proposed Elements of the Construction Outreach and Coordination Plan 

• Community Input Meetings • Task Force Development • Dedicated Webpage • Construction Updates and Notifications • CTA Business Outreach Program 

> Example of webpage outreach used during the CTA Brown Line Expansion Project
> Red-Purple Bypass Public Outreach Meeting, Spring 2014

# Community and Business Impacts Neighborhood Redevelopment Plan 

While the permanent result of these improvements is expected to be largely beneficial to the surrounding community, construction could have impacts to the community. Prior to construction, CTA will work with the City, Ward 44 alderman’s office, chambers of commerce, and the surrounding community to develop a plan for redevelopment after construction. 

Proposed Elements of the Neighborhood Redevelopment Plan 

• Identify development opportunities that fit within neighborhood context for excess property remaining after construction • Outline incentives to encourage redevelopment and minimize duration of vacant properties and parcels following construction 

Conceptual Rendering of Clark Street looking north toward Roscoe (Rendering depicts potential redevelopment) Conceptual rendering of Wilton Avenue looking northwest near Belmont station (Rendering depicts potential redevelopment) Visual and Aesthetic Changes 

The major visual and aesthetic changes proposed as part of the Red-Purple Bypass Project include the following: 

Fifth Track Bypass – Brown Line track would cross over the Red and Purple line tracks, clearing the tracks by approximately 22 feet at its highest point. At its highest point, the structure would be approximately 40 to 45 feet in height. 

> Photo and Artistic Conceptual Rendering of Proposed Red-Purple Bypass, Facing North from Belmont Station

Modern, Closed-Deck Structure and Noise Barriers – The proposed modern structure would have a closed deck, with noise barriers (approximately 3 to 5 feet high) on both sides of the track deck. The existing support structure (which uses riveted steel) would be replaced by a modern concrete or steel structure. 

Property Displacements – Property displacements would be required to accommodate the bypass, modernized mainline track structure, and construction. After construction, the remaining excess property will become available for potential redevelopment. Visual and Aesthetic Changes 

Existing Conditions Build Alternative (without redevelopment) Build Alternative (with redevelopment) 

Photo and Artistic Conceptual Rendering of Proposed Red-Purple Bypass with and without Redevelopment at Clark Street and Buckingham Place, Facing Northwest Visual and Aesthetic Changes 

Existing Conditions Build Alternative (without redevelopment) Build Alternative (with redevelopment) 

Photo and Artistic Conceptual Rendering of Proposed Red-Purple Bypass with and without Redevelopment at School Street and Wilton Avenue, Facing Southwest Visual and Aesthetic Changes 

Existing Conditions Build Alternative (with Vautravers Building moved and without redevelopment) Build Alternative (with Vautravers Building moved and redevelopment) 

Photo and Artistic Conceptual Rendering of Proposed Red-Purple Bypass with and without Redevelopment at Clark Street and Newport Avenue, Facing South Noise and Vibration Impacts Noise and Vibration Impacts 

• 70% of noise-sensitive areas near the Red-Purple Bypass would have reduced noise levels 

• At 6 of the 56 noise-sensitive receiver clusters identified, moderate or severe noise impacts and vibration increases were predicted due to trackwork (crossovers) or building demolition prior to mitigation 

Several noise- and vibration-reducing features are proposed as part of the Build Alternative, including a closed-deck structure, using welded rail, and installation of noise barriers. 

Noise and Vibration Mitigation 

• Design and construction mitigation measures will reduce noise and vibration levels to below FTA thresholds • Could include design measures such as low-impact frogs, rail dampers, rubber bearing pads, and other measures • Additional mitigation could include special track designs at crossovers or other measures to reduce noise levels • CTA will require the contractor to reduce construction noise and vibration with alternate operational scheduling, equipment choice, acoustical treatments, and by following best management practices 

> Closed Deck, Welded Rail with Noise Barriers

# Historic Resources 

The elevated track structure is individually eligible for the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) and would experience an adverse effect from implementation of this project. Implementation of the project would also result in adverse effects on one building and one National Register Historic District. 

> CTA Elevated Track Structure Vautravers Building
> 947-949 W. Newport Avenue
> Newport Avenue Historic District

Measures to Resolve Adverse Effects on Historic Resources 

Over the last year, FTA and CTA, in consultation with the Illinois Historic Preservation Agency and consulting parties, developed a series of measures to resolve the adverse effects, including the following: • CTA’s preferred option is to move the Vautravers Building approximately 29 feet to the west of the existing location • If not feasible to move the Vautravers Building, CTA will preserve key architectural features of the building • Develop and install an interpretive display conveying the history and significance of the north Red and Purple lines • Update historic documentation for the Newport Avenue Historic District • Prior to any demolition of historic resources, CTA will prepare appropriate historic record documentation Project Funding Overview Capital Investment Grant (CIG) Program 

• CTA intends to pursue funding from FTA for the Red-Purple Bypass Project. The CIG program involves a multiyear, multistep process that project sponsors must complete before a project is eligible for funding. 

Federal, State, and Local Funds 

• Federal funding could pay for a substantial portion of project costs, however state and local funds would still be needed to pay for more than half of project costs. • CTA is continuing to work with federal, state, and local agencies and elected officials to secure the necessary funding to keep this project moving forward with the support of the community. 

Cost Saving Strategies 

• CTA is also looking at cost-saving strategies through alternative construction and financing methods. Thank you for participating! Stay Involved 

• CTA and FTA will respond to public comments on the EA. • FTA will issue a NEPA Decision Document summarizing results of the EA including all comments and responses. • CTA will complete preliminary engineering in fall 2015. • CTA will apply to FTA to start the next phase of the Capital Investment Grant funding program (Engineering). • Once FTA’s NEPA decision is made, engineering is complete, and funding is secured, CTA will begin construction of this project. Contingent on these factors, construction could begin as early as late 2017. 

Next Steps

CTA Customers Enjoy Ceremonial “First Ride” on the New Red, Purple Line Elevated Tracks, Including Stops at the New, Fully Accessible Bryn Mawr and Berwyn Stations as Part of CTA’s Historic Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project
==================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================

 July 20, 2025 

 July 20, 2025 

 Staff 

**_The opening of four contiguous Red Line stations marks the first time that this many stations have opened at once since the Orange Line opened in 1993_**

CTA today opened its new Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn and Bryn Mawr Red Line stations as part of the $2.1 billion Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project and, to mark the special occasion, CTA celebrated with customers on a commemorative “first ride” train between the new Bryn Mawr and Berwyn Red Line stations.

CTA customers will enjoy the following amenities at the new stations:

*   Larger stations that replace stations that were more than 100 years old
*   ADA accessibility, including escalators, elevators and wider platforms
*   Better lighting and security features
*   Real-time information boards
*   Smoother, more reliable train service
*   Decrease in overcrowding on the trains and platforms
*   A brighter, cleaner and more aesthetically pleasing pedestrian environment
*   Original artwork at each station

RPM Phase One is the largest completed transit investment in CTA history, and the opening of four new contiguous stations marks the first time that this many stations have opened simultaneously since the Orange Line in 1993.

“It was wonderful to welcome CTA riders today to our brand new, fully accessible Red Line stations and to showcase the RPM team’s hard work to modernize and improve rail service for the people who visit, live in and work in these communities,” said Acting President Nora Leerhsen. “I am grateful to the people in the neighborhoods that these stations will serve— including the residents, businesses and local elected officials that have partnered with us during construction—for their support. Now is the time to celebrate together the access and opportunity that these new, breathtaking stations will provide.”

#### **RPM Phase One Overview**

RPM Phase One Project construction began in 2019 and includes three major components.

*   Reconstruction of the Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr Red Line stations into larger, fully accessible stations; and replacement of track structure totaling six track-miles. 
    *   The RPM project completely rebuilt century-old elevated track structure and replaced the signal system. The work included new track, support structures, bridges, and viaducts built along the 1.3-mile Lawrence to Bryn Mawr corridor, replacing century-old, deteriorated structures.

*   The new track bridge’s design provides improved sightlines for pedestrians and vehicles at cross streets under new viaducts with the elimination of columns in the middle of the street.
*   The new elevated structure is constructed higher to meet modern clearance standards.
*   The new signal system provides more reliable train service and replaces a more than 60-year-old system.

*   New Red-Purple Bypass construction and the reconstruction of Red and Purple Line track structure between Belmont and Newport/Cornelia.
*   Installation of a new signal system on 23 track miles between Howard and Belmont that, similar to roadway traffic signals, will improve train flow and service reliability.

#### **Public Space Under the ‘L’ Tracks**

With the completion of track and station construction, CTA will continue with some final finishing construction work and be substantially done with RPM Phase One by the end of 2025, with the exception of upcoming development of newly created under-L spaces:

*   CTA plans to develop 10 blocks of open space located under the new Red and Purple Line tracks between Lawrence and Ardmore avenues based on input from the community.
*   The open space design plans include a pedestrian trail, dog parks, playground, fitness area, benches, and flexible-use plaza space for community events.
*   Construction is expected to begin in 2026 and be completed in 2027.

#### **The Red Line and RPM**

The CTA’s Red Line is CTA’s busiest rail line, providing nearly 40 million rides in 2024. CTA is completing Phase One of the multi-phase RPM Program, which is rebuilding the 9.6-mile stretch of Red and Purple Line track structure and stations on the North Side that were a century old. RPM replaces aging infrastructure; increases CTA’s capacity to increase train service as needed; and improves our service for customers with more reliable, comfortable service. Learn more about RPM at [transitchicago.com/RPM](https://www.transitchicago.com/rpm/).

8.description: The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) corridor is a 9.6 mile stretch of track that was built close to a century ago. CTA needs to increase service on the Red Line to serve more riders, yet with current infrastructure constraints it has reached capacity.

About the RPM

 Phase One Project
=================================

![Image 14: LOGO_home](https://www.transitchicago.com/assets/1/6/LOGO_home.png)

The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project is the second-largest capital project in CTA history, consisting of a new bypass structure just north of the Belmont station, a complete rebuild of the Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn and Bryn Mawr stations and the installation of a new signal system between Howard and Belmont.

While large-scale mega-projects of this type come with benefits, such as smoother, more reliable service, relief of overcrowding and larger, modern stations with ADA accessibility, they also come with unique challenges due to their longevity and complexity. Recognizing that there will be challenges, CTA has taken a conscientious approach to construction and working closely with each of the communities and its leaders to minimize negative impacts.
